questions.explanation: \(A_{DM} = G_mR_{out} = g_m(r_{o2}\parallel r_{o4}) = 1\ \mathrm{mS}\times50\ \mathrm{k\Omega} = 50\). Positive with this output: raising \(v_{i1}\) makes the mirror push more current into the output while M2 pulls less.

questions.prompt: Order how a current-mirror load delivers the full differential transconductance to one output. \(v_{id}\) is the difference of the two gate voltages, and each input device has transconductance \(g_m\). Each step after the first uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: Resistor loads leave one drain with only its own \(g_m v_{id}/2\). The mirror turns the other half around and adds it, which is why \(G_m = g_m\). The tail current does not change under a pure differential input, and the tail is still what sets the sum. The two drains are not made identical: one side is a diode and the other is the high-impedance output. Half-circuit gain formulas do not apply to this asymmetric load.
steps: A differential input raises one input current by \(g_m v_{id}/2\) and lowers the other by the same amount.
The diode-connected transistor takes the increased current, and the mirror copies that increase into the output node.
The other input device's decrease is already leaving that same output node.
The two changes add, so the short-circuit output current is \(g_m v_{id}\), not half of it.

questions.prompt: Write the small-signal output resistance of a mirror-loaded pair, looking into the joined drains of the input device and the mirror device. Use ro2 and ro4.
questions.explanation: The two drains share the output node, so \(R_{out} = r_{o2}\parallel r_{o4} = r_{o2}r_{o4}/(r_{o2}+r_{o4})\). Adding \(r_{o2}+r_{o4}\) puts the two resistances in series. \(1/g_{m3}\) is the resistance of the diode-connected side, not of this node. \(R_{SS}\) is the tail, behind the sources. An external load connects to this node afterward; it is not already inside \(R_{out}\).

questions.prompt: Short the output to AC ground. With \(g_m = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\) for the input devices, what is the stage's transconductance \(G_m = i_{out}/v_{id}\) in mS?
questions.explanation: Half of \(v_{id}\) drives each side; M1's current is mirrored and adds to M2's change: \(i_{out} = g_mv_{id}\), so \(G_m = g_m = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\).

questions.explanation: Equal currents and gate voltages make M3 and M4 operate identically; in practice the high-impedance output is set by feedback around the amplifier.

questions.prompt: A worked solution analyses a mirror-loaded pair with half circuits. Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: A diode on one side and a current source on the other are not mirror images, so the modes mix. Substituting \(1/g_m\) for the diode does not make a legal half circuit. An ideal tail does not repair the asymmetry. \(G_m\) and \(R_{out}\) on the whole circuit are the small-signal description that remains. The gain is not \(g_m/2\); that factor belongs to one resistor-loaded drain.
steps: One load device is diode-connected, and the other is the mirror's output transistor.
Half circuits require the two halves to be mirror images, so a common-mode input produces no differential output.
Replacing the diode with \(1/g_m\) and cutting the circuit down the middle restores that symmetry.
The stage is instead read from \(G_m = g_m\) and from \(R_{out} = r_{o2}\parallel r_{o4}\) at the single output.
reasons: The loads are not symmetric, so the modes mix. \(G_m\) and \(R_{out}\) replace the half circuits.
A diode becomes \(1/g_m\), and that substitution is enough to keep the differential half circuit valid.

questions.prompt: In a mirror-loaded pair with input common-mode voltage 1.0 V and \(V_T = 0.4\ \mathrm{V}\), what is the lowest output voltage (V) that keeps M2 saturated?
questions.explanation: M2 needs \(V_D \ge V_G - V_T = 1.0 - 0.4 = 0.6\ \mathrm{V}\). The top of the swing is set by the PMOS: \(V_{DD} - |V_{ov4}|\).

questions.prompt: Preview of op-amp models: which simple model describes a mirror-loaded pair as an op-amp's first stage?
options: A transconductor \(G_m = g_m\) driving an output resistance \(r_{o2}\parallel r_{o4}\)
A current amplifier with zero output resistance
questions.explanation: That OTA model is the building block of two-stage op-amps.

questions.prompt: Preview of gain-bandwidth: the stage (\(G_m = 1\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(R_{out} = 50\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\)) drives \(C_L = 1\ \mathrm{pF}\). Find its unity-gain frequency in MHz.
questions.explanation: \(f_u \approx G_m/(2\pi C_L) = 159\ \mathrm{MHz}\), independent of \(R_{out}\), which only sets the DC gain and the pole.

questions.prompt: Preview of offsets: why does a mirror-loaded pair have a systematic offset even with perfect matching, if the output sits far from the diode node's voltage?
options: Because the tail current is ideal
Different \(V_{SD}\) on M3 and M4 changes their currents through \(\lambda\)
Because the input devices are NMOS
questions.explanation: The mirror copies exactly only when M4's drain voltage equals M3's.
